{
 "id": "Q03",
 "sourceFile": "Sports injuries and game stakes - Concussions in the National Football League.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text ('Sports injuries and game stakes: Concussions in the National Football League') matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["American Football"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Observational analysis of NFL regular-season games from 2012 to 2015 (948 games, 563 concussions after exclusions), with concussions taken from public injury reports. The authors measure game stakes as how much a win changes a team's playoff qualification odds, and control for fixed effects with standard errors clustered by team. They report that a game where a win guarantees playoff qualification is associated with a 24 percentage point higher risk of at least one concussion.",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is an observational panel analysis, so it shows association and not causation, and unmeasured game factors may be linked to stakes. Concussion counts depend on the public injury reports, which may miss or misclassify events, and the sample is four NFL seasons only.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the 24 point figure as the concussion risk in any high-stakes game, when it is one league's regular-season estimate built on a model-based measure of playoff odds.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2023,
   "citation": "Courty P, Cisyk J. Sports injuries and game stakes: Concussions in the National Football League. Economic Inquiry. 2023;1-19.",
   "doi": "10.1111/ecin.13173",
   "abstract": "NFL regular-season games differ in importance for playoff qualification. The authors build an incentive-based measure of how a win changes a team's qualification probability and relate it to concussions. Teams were 24 percentage points more likely to suffer a concussion in games where a win secures a playoff berth.",
   "tldr": "Concussion risk in NFL games appears higher when a win would secure playoff qualification. This is an observational finding from one league, so it should prompt readiness for high-stakes games rather than a firm risk estimate.",
   "methods": "Team-game panel of NFL regular-season games from 2012 to 2015, excluding neutral-site games and the final week. A swing measure of playoff odds was computed for each game, concussion events were taken from injury reports, and regressions included fixed effects with standard errors clustered by team.",
   "findings": "The swing variable had a statistically significant association with concussion incidence. A game that guarantees one team playoff qualification with a win was associated with a 24 percentage point higher risk of at least one concussion. Some alternative specifications gave weaker results.",
   "limitations": "Observational design with no direct measure of game intensity or exposure. The stakes measure depends on a model of playoff odds. Injury data come from public reports, and the findings are limited to NFL regular-season games from 2012 to 2015.",
   "practicalImplications": "Concussion risk may rise in games where the stakes are high, so staff could plan extra sideline and concussion-protocol readiness for those games. The paper does not test any prevention measure.",
   "athleteDev": "This paper does not address athlete development or performance. It covers injury risk linked to game stakes only.",
   "rtp": "This study does not inform return to sport. It measures how often concussions occur in high-stakes games and says nothing about recovery time or clearance decisions."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q04",
 "sourceFile": "Sports performance - is there evidence that the body clock plays a role.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text ('Sports performance: is there evidence that the body clock plays a role?') matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of the time-of-day pattern in athletic performance and whether the internal body clock contributes to it. It draws on laboratory and simulated-competition studies of strength, power, running, swimming, cycling and skilled tasks. The authors report performance peaks at about 15:30 to 20:30 hours, with amplitudes of 2 to 11 percent of the daily mean in studies that sampled at least six times across 24 hours.",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is a narrative review with no described search method, so the choice of studies cannot be checked. The authors note that much of the cited work is short-duration and of poor quality, and that the body clock cannot yet be separated from time awake and environmental factors.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the evening performance peak as proof that the body clock drives it, when the authors say current evidence cannot separate the body clock from sleep, time awake and environmental cues.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2009,
   "citation": "Reilly T, Waterhouse J. Sports performance: is there evidence that the body clock plays a role? Eur J Appl Physiol. 2009;106:321-332.",
   "doi": "10.1007/s00421-009-1066-x",
   "abstract": "Athletic performance shows a time-of-day effect with possible causes in environmental factors, the sleep-wake cycle and the internal body clock. The authors conclude that the body clock probably plays some role in sports performance rhythms, but the evidence does not separate it from time awake. They outline protocols to separate these roles and note that muscle fatigue is a serious barrier to experimental work.",
   "tldr": "Sports performance follows a time-of-day pattern that peaks in the late afternoon, and the body clock probably contributes to it. Current evidence cannot yet say how much of the pattern is the body clock rather than time awake or the environment.",
   "methods": "Narrative review of the time-of-day performance literature and chronobiological evidence, with suggested experimental protocols. No systematic search method is described.",
   "findings": "Many performance measures are higher in the late afternoon and early evening than in the morning. Reported rhythm peaks fall between about 15:30 and 20:30 hours, with amplitudes of 2 to 11 percent of the daily mean. The authors judge that the body clock probably plays some role, but the evidence is inconclusive.",
   "limitations": "Many of the cited studies are short-duration tasks of poor quality with small or unbalanced designs. Muscle fatigue makes rigorous protocols long or unacceptable, and the body clock and time awake cannot yet be separated.",
   "practicalImplications": "When comparing athlete performance across the day, standardise and record test times, because the time of day alone can shift results. Where possible, test protocols should separate time awake from the body clock.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance measures tend to peak in the late afternoon and early evening, so training and testing schedules could take time of day into account. This review cannot say how much of that rhythm is the body clock.",
   "rtp": "This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It does not address injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q06",
 "sourceFile": "Sprint running- from fundamental mechanics to practice—a review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text ('Sprint running: from fundamental mechanics to practice - a review') matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Track & Field", "Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Invited narrative review that applies fundamental mechanical principles to sprint running research. It assesses spring-mass models, force and power analyses based on total and horizontal (end-goal) force, and common coaching concepts. The authors argue that some models and power calculations from isolated horizontal force can lead to misinterpretation.",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is a narrative review with no described search method, so the choice of literature cannot be checked. It is largely a theoretical argument and reports no new athlete data.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat a model that fits sprint kinematics as proof of the underlying mechanism, which the authors say a model cannot establish.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2019,
   "citation": "Haugen T, McGhie D, Ettema G. Sprint running: from fundamental mechanics to practice (a review). Eur J Appl Physiol. 2019.",
   "doi": "10.1007/s00421-019-04139-0",
   "abstract": "The authors examine sprint running literature using the mechanical principles that govern accelerated running. They discuss spring-mass models and their limits, the link between sprint mechanics and metabolic demand, and the emphasis on total and horizontal force. They argue that power analysis based on isolated end-goal force is flawed and discuss some practical concepts in sprint coaching.",
   "tldr": "Sprint mechanics research can be misread when models or horizontal-force power figures are taken at face value. Coaches and analysts should check how a measure was derived before using it to explain sprint performance.",
   "methods": "Invited narrative review of sprint running mechanics literature, interpreted through fundamental mechanical principles. No systematic search method is described.",
   "findings": "Spring-mass models describe gross sprint kinematics such as step length, step rate and contact time, but the authors argue they have flaws when applied to accelerated running. Analyses based on total and horizontal force, and power derived from isolated end-goal force, are argued to be limited or flawed. Metabolic models of sprinting are described as promising but still model based.",
   "limitations": "The review is an argument rather than a systematic synthesis, and no search method is described. It presents no new data, and its views on practical sprint concepts are discussed rather than tested.",
   "practicalImplications": "Check how a sprint model or force measure was derived before treating it as a mechanism. Interpret horizontal-force power figures obtained from isolated force data with caution.",
   "athleteDev": "The mechanical principles can guide sprint technique and force-application work. Model-based power figures should not be read as direct measures of an athlete's capacity, and the review gives no training prescription.",
   "rtp": "This review does not address return to sport or rehabilitation and cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria."
 }
}
